title: The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
summary: The instruction cycle every CPU runs, one instruction at a time, before pipelining ever overlaps it.

slides.markdown:
Every CPU, at its core, repeats one loop forever: **fetch** the next instruction, **decode** what it means, **execute** it (which may include a memory access and a write-back). Then it does it again, for the next instruction.

This is true whether the chip is a decades-old microcontroller or a modern superscalar processor — the fancier chips just overlap and reorder many of these cycles at once (pipelining, out-of-order execution). Understanding the plain, one-at-a-time cycle first is what makes those later optimizations make sense.

The cycle literally feeds back into itself through the program counter:

![The fetch-decode-execute cycle as a loop feeding back into the program counter](assets/fetch-decode-execute-loop.svg)

After each instruction executes, the PC updates — normally by advancing to the next instruction, or by jumping elsewhere if the instruction was a taken branch — and the loop begins again with the new PC value.

assets.alt: The fetch-decode-execute cycle as a loop feeding back into the program counter

slides.markdown:
The **program counter (PC)** holds the address of the next instruction to fetch. In the ordinary case it simply advances by one instruction's width each cycle — `PC += 4` on a 32-bit fixed-length ISA.

A **taken branch or jump redirects it** instead — the execute stage computes a new target address and writes it into the PC, overriding the default "just advance" behavior. This single register is what makes a program's control flow possible: every loop, `if`, and function call ultimately works by changing what the PC does next.

**Fetch** reads the instruction word from memory at the address the PC holds — typically served from an instruction cache, not main memory directly, since fetch happens every single cycle and RAM is far too slow for that rate.

The fetched bits are just a number at this point; the CPU has no idea yet what operation they represent. That interpretation is entirely the next stage's job.

**Decode** extracts the opcode and operand fields from the fetched bit pattern, and reads any needed values out of the **register file** using the register-number fields.

By the end of decode, the CPU knows exactly *what* operation to do and has the actual operand values in hand — the execute stage doesn't need to interpret any more bits, just act on already-resolved values.

This chapter's cycle runs **one instruction fully to completion before the next one starts anything**. Pipelining changes the scheduling, not the steps themselves:

| | This cycle (single-instruction) | Pipelined version |
|---|---|---|
| Stages | Fetch, decode, execute (same list) | Same stages, same order |
| Overlap | None — one instruction at a time | Multiple instructions in different stages at once |
| Throughput | One instruction per full cycle-set | Close to one instruction per clock, once full |

Pipelining ([pipelining-fundamentals](pipelining-fundamentals)) is the same recipe run on an assembly line instead of one cook finishing a whole dish before starting the next.

slides.subTitle: What "execute" actually covers
slides.markdown:
"Execute" is really shorthand for up to three sub-steps, and not every instruction needs all of them. **Execute** proper runs the ALU on the decoded operand values (an add, a comparison, an address computation). **Memory** access only happens for loads and stores — a register-to-register `add` skips this step entirely. **Write-back** stores the result into the destination register, when there is one (a `store` writes to memory instead, and has no register write-back at all).

This is exactly why a `load` genuinely does more hardware work per instruction than an `add`: it uses execute (to compute the address), memory (to read the value), and write-back (to save it into a register) — three sub-steps where an `add` uses execute and write-back but skips memory.

slides.sectionTitle: Tracing one instruction end to end
slides.subTitle: A worked example
slides.markdown:
```text
Instruction: lw $t0, 8($s0)     ; load word from address ($s0 + 8) into $t0
Before: PC=0x1000, $s0=0x2000, Mem[0x2008]=42

Fetch:     read instruction word at PC=0x1000; PC_next = 0x1004
Decode:    opcode=LW, rs=$s0 (value 0x2000), rt=$t0, imm=8
Execute:   effective address = $s0 + imm = 0x2000 + 8 = 0x2008
Memory:    read Mem[0x2008] -> 42
Write-back: $t0 <- 42

After: $t0=42, PC=0x1004
```

Every field decode extracted in step 2 gets used by exactly one later stage — the register value feeds execute's address math, the computed address feeds memory, and the loaded value feeds write-back. Nothing is wasted, and nothing is used out of order.

slides.subTitle: When does the PC actually update?
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The PC only changes after execute finishes, once the CPU knows whether the instruction was a taken branch."

**Why it's wrong:** the **default PC+4 (or PC+instruction-width) increment happens during fetch**, immediately, well before decode even knows what the instruction is — the CPU speculatively assumes "no branch" and moves on. Only if execute later determines the instruction *was* a taken branch or jump does it overwrite that already-advanced PC with the real target.

**Correct model:** the sequential PC+width update is the default, computed early and optimistically; a taken branch is the exception that corrects it afterward. This ordering (increment first, correct later if wrong) is also exactly the setup that pipelined CPUs exploit and must handle carefully — it's the root of the branch-misprediction penalty covered in pipelining topics.
